subject: biology
title: Required practical: sampling with quadrats and transects
key_idea: Ecologists sample a habitat because they cannot count every organism. **Random quadrats** estimate the population size of a species. A **transect** shows how distribution changes along a line, for example away from a woodland.

blocks.text: A habitat is usually too large to count every organism. Instead, scientists count a sample. This section covers how to take a fair random sample.

items.meaning: A square frame, often 1 m by 1 m or 0.25 m², that marks out a known area to sample.
How many individuals of a species there are in an area.
Where in a habitat a species is found.
A sample where every part of the area has an equal chance of being chosen.

diagram.alt: Put the steps for estimating a population with random quadrats in order.
diagram.prompt: Put the steps for estimating a population size in order.
steps: Mark out the whole area and measure its length and width
Place a quadrat at random coordinates
Count the organisms in the quadrat
Repeat with a large number of quadrats
Calculate the mean number per quadrat
Scale up to the area of the whole field

items: Choose positions at random, for example with random coordinates from a calculator. This avoids bias.
Use a large number of quadrats, such as 10 or more, so the sample is representative.
Use the same size of quadrat each time.
Sampling only one part, such as the centre, may miss plants that grow elsewhere.
A quadrat marks a known area. Place it at random, many times.
A larger number of random samples gives a more representative result.

blocks.text: Use the mean count per quadrat, and the area of the whole habitat, to estimate the population.

items: **Mean:** add up all the counts and divide by the number of quadrats.
**Median:** the middle value when the counts are put in order.
**Mode:** the value that occurs most often.

blocks.label: Mean number per quadrat
blocks.formula: mean = total number of organisms counted ÷ number of quadrats

blocks.label: Estimated population size
blocks.formula: population size = mean number per m² × total area of the habitat
where: mean number per m², in organisms per m²

blocks.text: If a quadrat is not 1 m², first convert the mean count into the number per m².

diagram.alt: Estimate the size of a population from the mean number per square metre and the area of a rectangular field.
diagram.question: A quadrat of area 1 m² is placed at random many times in a rectangular field measuring {L} m by {W} m. The mean number of ragwort plants per quadrat is {m}. Estimate the number of ragwort plants in the field.
working: Population size = mean per m² × area = {m} × {L} × {W}

items: Mean per quadrat, then multiply by the total area.
Use length × width to find the area of a rectangular field.

sections.heading: Using a transect to investigate distribution

blocks.text: A random sample shows how many organisms there are. A transect shows how their numbers change from place to place.

rows: Estimating how many of a species there are in an area
Investigating how distribution changes along a line, such as away from a woodland
At regular intervals along a line
Measure the factor, such as light intensity, at each quadrat

items.text: Place a tape measure in a straight line from the edge of the woodland out into the field.
Put a quadrat against the tape at regular intervals.
Count the organisms of the species in each quadrat.
Measure the abiotic factor, such as light intensity, at each quadrat.
See whether the number of organisms changes as the factor changes.

items: A transect samples along a line to show how distribution changes.
Measure the factor at every quadrat so the results can be compared.

checks.q: Describe how a quadrat is used to estimate the population of a plant species in a field.
checks.a: Place the quadrat at random positions (for example using random coordinates). Count the plants in each quadrat. Use a large number of quadrats and calculate the mean per quadrat (or per m²). Multiply by the area of the field.

checks.q: A field is 40 m by 25 m. The mean number of daisies per m² is 3. Estimate the population of daisies.
Describe how a transect could be used to investigate the effect of light intensity on the distribution of a plant.
checks.a: Lay a line from the edge of the woodland. Place a quadrat at regular distances along it and count the plants in each. Measure the light intensity at each quadrat. Compare the numbers with the light intensity.

exam_phrases: quadrats are placed randomly
random coordinates from a calculator
suitable number of quadrats (10 or more or a large number)
count number of plants (in each quadrat)
calculation of mean per quadrat or per unit area
determination of area of field (length x width)
population = mean per m² x area of field

for each quadrat measure light intensity

mistakes.wrong: Place one quadrat in a shady area and one in a sunny area.
mistakes.right: A large number of quadrats is needed, placed randomly or at intervals along a transect, so that the outcome is valid.

mistakes.wrong: Place the quadrats in places where the plants are growing.
mistakes.right: Placing must be random. Give a method, such as random coordinates from a calculator, or a throw over the shoulder.

mistakes.wrong: Count the plants in one quadrat to get the population of the field.
mistakes.right: Find the mean per quadrat or per m², then multiply by the area of the field, which is length × width.

worked_example.question:
Ragwort is a weed that grows on farmland. Ragwort is poisonous to horses.

Plan an investigation to estimate the size of a population of ragwort growing in a rectangular field on a farm.
answer_points: Use a quadrat of known area, for example 1 m × 1 m or 0.25 m².
Place the quadrats randomly, using a method such as random coordinates from a calculator.
Use a suitable number of quadrats, such as 10 or more.
Count the number of plants in each quadrat.
Calculate the mean per quadrat or per unit area.
Work out the area of the field (length × width).
Population = mean per m² × area of the field.
worked_example.tip: Marked by level. A valid plan has all the key steps in a logical order.

exam_phrases: place a line (at 90°) from the edge of the forest
place a quadrat against the line
count / record the number of species / plants (in the quadrat)
measure the light (intensity)
move along the line / repeat at different distances
use a light meter / lux meter
multiplication factor to make the estimate

mistakes.wrong: Place a quadrant along the tape measure.
mistakes.right: "Quadrant" is rejected. The apparatus is a quadrat.

mistakes.wrong: Count the slugs in the quadrat. This is the population of slugs in the garden.
mistakes.right: A multiplication factor is needed to scale up the count from the sampled area to the whole garden.

worked_example.question:
A scientist observes that trees at the edge of a forest shade part of a field.

Describe how a belt transect could be used to see how light intensity affects the biodiversity of plants growing in the field.
answer_points: Place a line (at 90°) from the edge of the forest.
Place a quadrat against the line.
Count or record the number of species (or plants) in the quadrat.
Move along the line, or repeat at different distances from the forest.
worked_example.tip: Any three score one mark each.

exam_phrases: position at random
random number generator / grid references / co-ordinates
count the number (of plants in a quadrat)
repeat / use of several quadrats
mean = divide (total) number by number of quadrats
scaling up to the number in 1 m²
capture some butterflies, mark and release them
key to identify species of plants
only sampled in the centre of the marsh / less representative

mistakes.wrong: The gardener uses a transect line to estimate the number of plants per m².
mistakes.right: A transect line is not allowed here. Use a quadrat, positioned at random.

mistakes.wrong: Count the percentage cover of the plants in the quadrat.
mistakes.right: Percentage cover is ignored when the question asks for the number. Count the number of plants in the quadrat.

mistakes.wrong: Five quadrats placed close together in the centre give a good sample.
mistakes.right: This samples less area and is not random. The centre may have different plants from the edges, so the results are less representative.

worked_example.question:
Some students investigate the number of dandelion plants growing in three different parts of a football pitch. The students sample the pitch to find the mean number of dandelion plants per m² in each part.

Explain how the students use a quadrat to find the mean number of dandelion plants per m² in a part of the pitch.
answer_points: Position the quadrat at random in that part of the pitch (random number generator, grid references or co-ordinates).
Count the number of dandelions in the quadrat.
Mean = total number of dandelions divided by the number of quadrats.
worked_example.tip: Any three points score one mark each. A transect line is not accepted for the quadrat point.

blocks.text: Animals move, so quadrats do not work well. Capture-recapture estimates the size of an animal population.

items.text: Catch a sample of animals, for example butterflies in nets.
Mark each animal harmlessly and release it.
After a period of time catch a second sample. Count how many are marked.
Use the equation to estimate the population.

blocks.label: Population size (capture-recapture)
blocks.formula: population size = (number marked in first sample × size of second sample) ÷ number recaptured
where: number marked in first sample, in animals
size of second sample, in animals
number recaptured (marked animals in the second sample), in animals

blocks.text: For example, 20 marked, a second sample of 30 and 5 recaptured gives 20 × 30 ÷ 5 = 120 animals.

items: Plants do not move, so they are easy to count with quadrats.
Animals can move away, or be counted twice, or be missed if they burrow.
A pooter or a pitfall trap can be used to catch small animals.
